board_asks: finding the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial and verifying the sum/product relationship with its coefficients, reading the number of zeroes off a graph (the geometrical meaning), and forming a quadratic from a given sum and product of zeroes.

big_idea.tagline: Zeroes are where the graph lands on the x-axis.
big_idea.body: A polynomial's zeroes are the values of $x$ that make it $0$ - and geometrically, they are exactly the points where the graph $y=p(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis. This short chapter ties three views of one idea together: the algebra (factorise to find the zeroes), the geometry (count the $x$-axis crossings), and the coefficients (for a quadratic, $\alpha+\beta=-\dfrac{b}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta=\dfrac{c}{a}$). Master the quadratic case - that is what the board assesses.

definitions.verbatim: Recall that if p(x) is a polynomial in x, the highest power of x in p(x) is called the degree of the polynomial p(x).
definitions.plain: the highest power of the variable. $4x+2$ has degree 1; $2y^2-3y+4$ has degree 2. Degree tells you the polynomial's family - and caps how many zeroes it can have.

definitions.verbatim: More generally, any quadratic polynomial in x is of the form ax2 + bx + c, where a, b, c are real numbers and a ≠ 0.
definitions.plain: a degree-2 polynomial, $ax^2+bx+c$ with $a\neq 0$. This is the case the whole chapter (and the board) focuses on.

definitions.verbatim: More generally, a real number k is said to be a zero of a polynomial p(x), if p(k) = 0.
definitions.plain: a value of $x$ that makes the polynomial equal $0$. Same idea as a root of the equation $p(x)=0$. Note: a zero is not the value $p(0)$.

definitions.verbatim: the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial ax2 + bx + c, a ≠ 0, are precisely the x-coordinates of the points where the parabola representing y = ax2 + bx + c intersects the x-axis.
definitions.plain: draw $y=p(x)$ and look at where it meets the $x$-axis - each crossing is a zero. This is why the number of zeroes can be read straight off a graph.

definitions.verbatim: If p(x) is a polynomial in x, and if k is any real number, then the value obtained by replacing x by k in p(x), is called the value of p(x) at x = k, and is denoted by p(k).
A polynomial of degree 1 is called a linear polynomial.
A polynomial of degree 3 is called a cubic polynomial.

concepts.title: Zeroes of a polynomial
concepts.body: A zero of $p(x)$ is any value $k$ with $p(k)=0$ - substitute it and the polynomial collapses to $0$. For a quadratic, factorise $ax^2+bx+c$ into two linear factors and set each to zero; the two values you get are the zeroes.
concepts.tested: 1-mark 'is $k$ a zero of $p(x)$?' and 2-mark 'find the zeroes'.

concepts.title: Geometrical meaning - zeroes are x-axis crossings
concepts.body: The zeroes of $p(x)$ are exactly the $x$-coordinates where the graph $y=p(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis. A parabola $y=ax^2+bx+c$ can meet the axis at two points (two distinct zeroes), touch it at one point (two equal zeroes), or miss it entirely (no zero).
concepts.tested: 1-mark MCQ 'number of zeroes from the graph' (Exercise 2.1 style).

concepts.title: A quadratic has at most two zeroes
concepts.body: Degree bounds the count: the graph of a degree-$n$ polynomial meets the $x$-axis at most $n$ times, so a quadratic has at most two zeroes and a linear polynomial has exactly one.
concepts.tested: Reasoning / MCQ on the maximum number of zeroes.

concepts.title: Zeroes and coefficients (quadratic)
concepts.body: For zeroes $\alpha,\beta$ of $ax^2+bx+c$: $\alpha+\beta=-\dfrac{b}{a}$ (sum) and $\alpha\beta=\dfrac{c}{a}$ (product). This lets you verify computed zeroes without solving again.
concepts.tested: 2-3 mark 'find the zeroes and verify the relationship' - the chapter's staple.

concepts.title: Building a quadratic from its zeroes
concepts.body: Given the sum $s$ and product $p$ of the zeroes, a quadratic is $x^2 - s\,x + p$ (and any real multiple $k$ of it also works). So sum $-3$, product $2$ gives $x^2+3x+2$.

examples.shape: Find zeroes + verify relationship · NCERT Example 2
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial x2 + 7x + 10, and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.

solution_steps.text: $x^2+7x+10=0$ when $x+2=0$ or $x+5=0$, i.e. $x=-2$ or $x=-5$. So the zeroes are $-2$ and $-5$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for the factorisation, 1 for stating BOTH zeroes, 1 for verifying sum $=-b/a$ and product $=c/a$. The verification is explicitly asked - skip it and the last mark is gone.

examples.shape: Irrational zeroes via a2-b2 · NCERT Example 3
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the zeroes of the polynomial x2 – 3 and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients.

solution_steps.text: $x^2-3=0$ when $x=\sqrt{3}$ or $x=-\sqrt{3}$. So the zeroes are $\sqrt{3}$ and $-\sqrt{3}$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for factorising with $a^2-b^2$, 1 for both zeroes $\pm\sqrt{3}$, 1 for the sum/product check (note $b=0$, so the sum is $0$).

examples.shape: Form a quadratic from sum & product · NCERT Example 4
examples.problem_verbatim: Find a quadratic polynomial, the sum and product of whose zeroes are – 3 and 2, respectively.

solution_steps.text: Let the polynomial be $ax^2+bx+c$ with zeroes $\alpha,\beta$: $\alpha+\beta=-3=-\dfrac{b}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta=2=\dfrac{c}{a}$.

solution_steps.lead: Choose a and read off the polynomial.
solution_steps.text: Take $a=1$, so $b=3$ and $c=2$. One polynomial that fits is $x^2+3x+2$; any $k(x^2+3x+2)$, $k$ real, also works.

examples.mark_logic: 2-mark shape: 1 for writing sum $=-b/a$ and product $=c/a$, 1 for the polynomial $x^2+3x+2$ (stating the general $k$-multiple earns the mark cleanly).

examples.shape: Find zeroes + verify · NCERT Exercise 2.2 Q1(i)
examples.problem_verbatim: Find the zeroes of the following quadratic polynomials and verify the relationship between the zeroes and the coefficients. (i) x2 – 2x – 8

solution_steps.text: $x-4=0$ or $x+2=0$, i.e. $x=4$ or $x=-2$. The zeroes are $4$ and $-2$.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark shape: 1 for factorising, 1 for both zeroes, 1 for verifying sum $=-b/a$ and product $=c/a$. (Solution authored to the standard 3-mark scheme; the problem is NCERT Exercise 2.2 Q1(i).)

strategies.text: Factorise the quadratic into two linear factors, set each to zero, and read off BOTH zeroes.
Check $\alpha+\beta=-\dfrac{b}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta=\dfrac{c}{a}$ - it is a separate mark, never skip it.
Use $x^2-(\text{sum})x+(\text{product})$; add that any real $k$-multiple also fits.
Count the points where the curve crosses the $x$-axis - that is the number of zeroes.
Compute $p(k)$; it is a zero exactly when $p(k)=0$.

pitfalls.text: Giving only one zero of a quadratic - always solve both linear factors and state both values.
Sign slip in the sum: $\alpha+\beta=-\dfrac{b}{a}$ carries a minus; the product $\alpha\beta=\dfrac{c}{a}$ does not.
Confusing a 'zero' with $p(0)$ - a zero is where $p(x)=0$, not where $x=0$.
Counting a touch-point as two crossings - when the parabola just touches the axis, that is two equal zeroes (one point), not two distinct ones.

branches.label: Zeroes of p(x)

third_tab_content.name: Zeroes & coefficients of a quadratic - why sum = -b/a and product = c/a
third_tab_content.intro: The relationship you use to verify zeroes is not a rule to memorise blindly - NCERT derives it by writing the quadratic in terms of its factors and comparing coefficients. The 2026-27 syllabus keeps this QUADRATIC relationship (the cubic version is out of scope).

steps.claim: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the zeroes of $p(x)=ax^2+bx+c$, then $(x-\alpha)$ and $(x-\beta)$ are its factors.
So $p(x)$ is a constant $k$ times the product of those factors.
Compare the coefficients of $x^2$, of $x$, and the constant term on both sides.
Divide through by $k=a$ to isolate the sum and product.
steps.justification: b/a and c/a fall straight out - this is exactly the relationship used to verify a pair of zeroes.
